group.title: The digital world
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Close, ongoing watching of people or places, often by a government or company.
examples: Critics warn that facial recognition makes mass {surveillance} far too easy.
wrong: The surveillance was so loose that nobody watched the building at all.

words.meaning: The state of not having your name or identity known to others.
examples: Many users value the {anonymity} that a nickname gives them online.
wrong: She gave up her anonymity by keeping her real name secret from everyone.

words.meaning: The practice of protecting computers, networks and data from attacks.
examples: The bank doubled its {cybersecurity} budget after the attack.
wrong: Good cybersecurity means leaving every account without a password.

words.meaning: Information that describes other data, such as when a photo was taken or who sent a message.
examples: Even without reading your messages, the {metadata} shows who you talk to and when.
wrong: The metadata was the actual text of the letter, not any details about it.

words.meaning: Harmful software that secretly watches what you do on a device and sends the details to someone else.
examples: The free game came bundled with {spyware} that recorded every key pressed.
wrong: Spyware is a tool that openly protects your privacy from trackers.

words.meaning: The ability of a device or place to connect to the internet or other systems.
examples: Rural areas still suffer from poor {connectivity}.
wrong: The village had excellent connectivity, so no phone could ever get online there.

words.meaning: To turn printed documents, pictures or sound into a form a computer can store.
examples: The library is {digitizing} its old newspapers so people can search them online.
wrong: They digitized the photos by printing them out on paper.

words.meaning: An incident in which private information is stolen or exposed without permission.
examples: After the {data breach}, millions of customers had to change their passwords.
wrong: The data breach kept every customer record perfectly safe and private.

words.meaning: A person who posts rude or annoying messages online on purpose to upset people.
examples: Don’t reply to that comment; it’s just a {troll} looking for attention.
wrong: The troll left kind, helpful replies to everyone on the forum.

words.meaning: An online space where people only hear opinions that match their own.
examples: If you only follow people who agree with you, your feed becomes an {echo chamber}.
wrong: The forum was an echo chamber because it was full of sharply opposing views.

words.meaning: A situation where websites only show you content that suits your past choices, hiding other views.
examples: Personalized news feeds can trap readers in a {filter bubble}.
wrong: Living in a filter bubble means you see a wide range of views you never chose.

words.meaning: Searching through large amounts of information with software to find patterns.
examples: The store uses {data mining} to predict what customers will buy next.
wrong: Data mining means deleting information without looking at it.

words.meaning: Hurting or frightening someone with messages or posts online.
examples: The school ran a campaign against {cyberbullying} on social media.
wrong: Her cyberbullying was a series of kind messages that cheered her friend up.

words.meaning: The trail of information you leave behind whenever you use the internet.
examples: Think before you post: your {digital footprint} can follow you for years.
wrong: He had no digital footprint because he posted online every single day.

words.meaning: To choose not to take part in something, such as a scheme or data collection.
examples: You can {opt out} of marketing emails in your account settings.
wrong: She opted out of the newsletter, so she now receives it every week.

words.meaning: To find a way to earn money from something, such as a website or video.
examples: The creator {monetized} her channel by adding adverts.
wrong: He monetized the app by making it free and removing every way to pay.

words.meaning: Finding out where a device or person is, using signals such as GPS or Wi-Fi.
examples: The app uses {geolocation} to show restaurants near you.
wrong: Geolocation hides your position so that no app can tell where you are.

words.meaning: A period when a service such as power or the internet is not working.
examples: The two-hour {outage} left thousands of people unable to pay online.
wrong: During the outage, the website worked faster than ever.

words.meaning: A person who checks posts on a website and removes ones that break the rules.
examples: The {moderator} deleted the abusive comments within minutes.
wrong: The moderator’s job is to post as many rule-breaking comments as possible.

words.meaning: A security method where only the sender and receiver can read a message, not the service in between.
examples: With {end-to-end encryption}, even the company cannot read your chats.
wrong: End-to-end encryption lets the service provider read every message you send.

words.meaning: A computer program that does tasks automatically, sometimes pretending to be a real person.
examples: Many of the accounts sharing the rumor turned out to be {bots}.
wrong: The bot was a real person typing every reply by hand.

words.meaning: A fake video or recording made with software so a real person seems to say or do something.
examples: The {deepfake} showed the mayor saying words she had never spoken.
wrong: The deepfake was a genuine, unedited recording of the event.

words.meaning: To change something so it suits one particular person’s interests or needs.
examples: The app {personalizes} your news feed based on what you read.
wrong: They personalized the service by giving every user exactly the same page.

words.meaning: To collect large amounts of personal data, often without people noticing.
examples: The game was secretly {harvesting} players’ contact lists.
wrong: The company harvested user data by refusing to collect any of it.

words.meaning: The gap between people who have easy access to computers and the internet and people who do not.
examples: Cheap tablets helped narrow the {digital divide} in poorer schools.
wrong: The digital divide means everyone has exactly the same internet access.

words.meaning: A person who grew up with the internet and smartphones and uses them naturally.
examples: As a {digital native}, she has never known life without online maps.
wrong: My grandfather is a digital native who first used a computer at seventy.

words.meaning: The number of hours a person spends looking at phones, computers or TV.
examples: Parents worry about how much {screen time} their children have.
wrong: She cut her screen time by watching more videos on her phone.

words.meaning: The rules you must agree to before you can use a website or app.
examples: Few people read the {terms of service} before clicking Accept.
wrong: The terms of service are the reviews other users write about the app.

words.meaning: Made by the people who use a website rather than by the company that runs it.
examples: The platform relies on {user-generated} videos rather than its own shows.
wrong: All the user-generated content was written by the company’s own staff.

words.meaning: To get ideas, work or money from a large number of people, usually online.
examples: The team {crowdsourced} translations of the guide from volunteers.
wrong: They crowdsourced the design by giving it to one expert alone.

words.meaning: A small file a website saves on your device to remember you and your activity.
examples: The site asks whether you accept {cookies} before you continue.
wrong: A cookie is a cable that connects your laptop to the screen.

words.meaning: A login method that asks for a second proof of identity, such as a code sent to your phone.
examples: Turn on {two-factor authentication} so a stolen password is not enough.
wrong: With two-factor authentication, you log in with no checks at all.

words.meaning: To get into a computer system or account without permission.
examples: Someone {hacked} his email and sent messages to all his contacts.
wrong: She hacked into her own account by typing her normal password.

words.meaning: The crime of using someone else’s personal details to pretend to be them, often to get money.
examples: After the data leak, several customers were victims of {identity theft}.
wrong: Identity theft is when you proudly show your own passport.

words.meaning: Done or decided by a set of computer rules rather than by people.
examples: Critics say {algorithmic} hiring can repeat old prejudices.
wrong: The ranking was algorithmic because an editor chose every item by hand.

words.meaning: The principle that internet providers should treat all online traffic equally.
examples: Supporters of {net neutrality} oppose paid fast lanes for big companies.
wrong: Under net neutrality, providers may slow down any website they dislike.

words.meaning: A hidden part of the internet that ordinary search engines cannot find, often used for illegal trade.
examples: The stolen card numbers were offered for sale on the {dark web}.
wrong: The dark web is the part of the internet that every search engine shows first.

words.meaning: Using body features such as fingerprints or faces to identify a person.
examples: The airport uses {biometric} scanners instead of checking boarding passes.
wrong: The biometric lock opens with a printed code, not any part of your body.

words.meaning: To read an online forum or group without ever posting anything yourself.
examples: I {lurked} on the forum for months before writing my first post.
wrong: He lurks in the chat by posting dozens of messages every hour.

words.meaning: Harmful software that locks your files until you pay money to the attacker.
examples: The {ransomware} demanded payment before staff could open their files.
wrong: Ransomware is a free program that backs up your photos for you.
